title: SEC1
lead: TryHackMe's hands-on beginner cert. There's no multiple choice: you work real tasks on a lab machine across red team, blue team and purple team scenarios. It proves you can use the basic tools of both sides (the command line, Wireshark, logs, password crackers, Burp) before you pick a lane like SAL1 or PT1.
objSub: Six skill areas from TryHackMe's SEC1 training content. Tick objectives as you study them; progress saves on this device.
planSub: Set how many hours a week you can give it. The plan splits about 50 hours across the six areas (the Cyber Security 101 path is the main prep), then saves the last stretch for timed practice in the labs.
pbqSub: Hands-on practice in the style of the exam: read what the tools show you and answer from the evidence.

cur.label: Current exam
cur.note: Seven sections spanning red, blue and purple team work, all answered from what you find on an analyst VM full of artifacts. Results are instant. One free retake comes with the exam. No prerequisites; TryHackMe recommends finishing the Cyber Security 101 path first.
cur.onote: Skill areas from TryHackMe's SEC1 training content. The lines under each are a plain-language breakdown, not an official list. TryHackMe publishes no weights, so the bars show an even split.

domains.name: Operating System Fundamentals
obj: Navigate Windows and Linux from the command line
PowerShell and cmd on Windows; bash, ls, cd, cat, grep and find on Linux.
Understand file systems and permissions
NTFS permissions, Linux rwx bits, owners and groups, and where key files live.
Manage users and groups
Local accounts, admin vs standard users, sudo and why least privilege matters.
Use built-in security features
Windows Defender, the firewall, UAC, Event Viewer, and Linux logs in /var/log.

domains.name: Network Traffic Analysis
obj: Explain how data moves across networks
IP addresses, ports, TCP vs UDP, the handshake, DNS and HTTP.
Capture and read packets
Filter and follow streams in Wireshark; quick looks with tcpdump.
Tell normal traffic from anomalous traffic
Scans, beaconing, odd ports, clear-text credentials and large transfers.

domains.name: Web Application Security
obj: Explain how web applications work
Requests and responses, methods, status codes, cookies and sessions.
Recognize common web vulnerabilities
Injection, cross-site scripting, broken access control and insecure direct object references.
Follow a basic web testing method
Map the site, inspect requests with a proxy like Burp, test inputs, and record findings, only with permission.

domains.name: Security Operations
obj: Analyze logs
Windows event logs, Linux auth logs and web server logs: who, what, when and from where.
Detect threats with monitoring tools
Search and correlate events in a SIEM; understand alerts and rules.
Identify incidents
Separate true positives from noise and know what to escalate.

domains.name: Password Attacks and Credential Security
obj: Explain brute-force and dictionary attacks
Online guessing vs offline cracking, wordlists and password spraying.
Crack password hashes in a lab
Identify a hash type and crack it with John the Ripper or Hashcat.
Recommend strong authentication
Length over complexity, password managers, lockouts and MFA.

domains.name: Malware Analysis Fundamentals
obj: Identify malware types and behaviors
Viruses, worms, trojans, ransomware, RATs and droppers, and what each does.
Perform basic static analysis
Hashes, strings, file headers and reputation lookups, without running the file.
Perform basic dynamic analysis
Run samples in a sandbox and watch processes, files, registry and network.

extras.title: Tools you'll reach for
rows: Filter with ip.addr==, http, dns; Follow TCP Stream.
Find the failed logins, the odd IP, the one bad line.
Catch and change requests between browser and site.
Turn a captured hash into a password, in a lab.
Fingerprint a sample and look it up.
Readable text in a binary: URLs, commands, names.

extras.title: Red, blue and purple
rows: Find and use weaknesses, with permission, to show the risk.
Watch logs and traffic, spot the attack and respond.
Use what the attack did to make the defense better.

extras.title: Work a hands-on question
extras.sub: A method that keeps you moving
rows: Read the scenario and the question twice. Note exactly what it asks for: an IP, a user, a flag, a time.
Find the right artifact first: the log, the PCAP, the file or the web page.
Narrow it down with filters and search, not by scrolling.
Write down each answer and where you found it before moving on.
Stuck for 15 minutes? Flag it, do the next section, come back fresh.

method: Use the six areas as your checklist and work through TryHackMe's Cyber Security 101 path in order.
Every room has tasks. Do them all in the AttackBox or your own VM; typing the commands is the study.
Keep a cheat sheet of commands, Wireshark filters and log locations. You'll use it on exam day.
Alternate red and blue rooms so you learn how each attack shows up in the logs.
Before booking, try a few rooms you haven't seen without hints, timed.
tips: 24 hours is plenty. Take breaks and come back to hard sections.
Every answer is in an artifact. If you're guessing, you haven't found the right file yet.
Hands-on answers are checked exactly. Copy and paste IPs, hashes and names instead of retyping.
Use these skills only in TryHackMe, your own lab, or with written permission.

items: The six skill areas, exam format and FAQ.
The prep path the exam is built on. Some rooms are free; Premium unlocks all.
Networking, web and OS basics if you're brand new.

quiz.q: On a Linux box you run ls -l and see: -rwxr-x--- 1 root ops 2048 report.sh. Who can run the script?
o: root and members of the ops group
Right. The owner (root) has rwx, the group (ops) has r-x, and everyone else has nothing.
The last three characters are ---, so other users have no access.
The group's x bit is set, so ops members can run it too.
x is set for the owner and the group.

quiz.q: Which Windows tool shows logon events like 4624 and 4625?
o: Event Viewer, in the Security log
Right. 4624 is a successful logon and 4625 a failed one.
It shows running processes and performance, not logon history.

quiz.q: In Wireshark you want only traffic to or from 10.10.5.20. Which display filter works?
o: Right. ip.addr matches the address as source or destination.
That's capture-filter (BPF) syntax, not a display filter.
Not valid. The field is ip.addr, ip.src or ip.dst.

quiz.q: A PCAP shows one host sending SYN packets to ports 1 through 1024 on another host, a few milliseconds apart, with almost no full connections. What is it?
o: Right. Many SYNs to many ports in a short time is a scan looking for open services.
Browsing uses a few ports, mostly 80 and 443, with full connections.
DNS is one small query to port 53.
A download is one long connection with lots of data.

quiz.q: A shop's URL is /order?id=1043. Changing it to id=1044 shows another customer's order. What is this?
o: Broken access control (an insecure direct object reference)
Right. The app doesn't check that the order belongs to the logged-in user.
XSS injects script into a page. Nothing was injected here.
No SQL was injected; a normal ID was simply changed.

quiz.q: A login form's response changes when you enter a single quote (') in the username, showing a database error. What does that suggest?
o: The input may be open to SQL injection
Right. A quote breaking the query means user input reaches the database unsanitized. Report it; test further only with permission.
The error comes from the username field and the database, not password rules.
Encryption has nothing to do with a database error.
A lockout gives a message, not a database error.

quiz.q: An auth log shows 300 failed SSH logins for different usernames from one IP in two minutes, then one success. What should you do FIRST?
o: Treat the success as a likely compromise: escalate it and check what that account did
Right. A burst of failures then a success suggests a brute-force attack worked.
Ignore it; failed logins are normal
300 in two minutes from one IP isn't normal, and one of them got in.
Delete the logs to save space
That doesn't stop an attacker with valid credentials and wipes some evidence.

quiz.q: What is the main job of a SIEM?
o: Collect logs from many sources, correlate them and alert on suspicious patterns
Right. That's how a SOC sees across endpoints, servers and network gear at once.
That's a web proxy or filter.

quiz.q: An attacker tries 'Spring2026!' against 500 accounts, once each. What attack is this?
o: Right. One common password across many accounts avoids per-account lockouts.
A dictionary attack on one account
That tries many passwords against one account.
Stuffing reuses real username and password pairs leaked from other sites.
Rainbow tables crack stolen hashes offline.

quiz.q: You captured the hash 5f4dcc3b5aa765d61d8327deb882cf99 in a lab. It's 32 hex characters. What is the MOST likely hash type?
o: Right. MD5 produces 128 bits, shown as 32 hex characters.
bcrypt hashes start with $2 and include a salt.

quiz.q: Which control does MOST to stop a stolen password from being enough to log in?
o: Right. The attacker also needs the second factor, like an app code or key.
Forcing a password change every 30 days
Frequent changes often lead to weaker, predictable passwords and don't stop immediate reuse.

quiz.q: You have a suspicious file. Which is a STATIC analysis step?
o: Hashing it and pulling out its readable strings
Right. Static analysis looks at the file without running it.
Running it in a sandbox and watching its network traffic
Opening it on your work laptop
That risks infecting a real system.

quiz.q: In a sandbox, a file encrypts documents and drops a note asking for Bitcoin. What type of malware is it?
o: Right. It encrypts data and demands payment.
Worms spread themselves across networks; encryption plus a ransom note is ransomware.

pbqs.title: What does each artifact show?
pbqs.scenario: Six artifacts from the analyst VM. Pick what each one shows. Each answer is used once; two options are distractors.

items.why: One source probing many ports in seconds is a port scan.

items.log:
Failed password for invalid user admin from 203.0.113.9
Failed password for invalid user test from 203.0.113.9
... (412 lines in 3 minutes)
items.why: Hundreds of failed logins from one IP in minutes is brute force.

items.log:
USER backupsvc
331 Password required
PASS Summer2026
230 Login successful
items.why: FTP sends usernames and passwords in clear text, readable in the capture.

items.log:
GET http://198.51.100.7/inv0ice.pdf.exe 200 2.4 MB
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0  user: jdoe
items.why: A double extension (.pdf.exe) from a bare IP is a classic malicious download.
' OR 1=1-- is a textbook SQL injection probe.
A Run key launching an unknown program at every logon is persistence.

pbqs.title: Pick the tool and the team
pbqs.scenario: For each task, pick the best tool and which team usually does it. Some options aren't used.

rows.req: Find which hosts and ports are open on a lab network
rows.why: Nmap discovers hosts and services. Attackers (and pentesters) start here.

rows.req: Change a request between the browser and a test website
rows.why: Burp's proxy lets you catch and edit requests.

rows.req: Crack a captured password hash in a lab
Follow a suspicious TCP stream in a capture
rows.why: Wireshark reads and reassembles traffic for defenders.

rows.req: Review failed logon events on a Windows server
rows.why: Event Viewer's Security log holds 4625 failed logons.

rows.req: Watch what an unknown file does when it runs
rows.why: A sandbox runs it safely so you can watch its behavior.
